meta.title: Who really said "What is necessary to change a person is to change his awareness of himself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No work of Maslow's has ever been cited for this line. Wikiquote files it under Attributed; the sole citation points to a 1972 juvenile science book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'What is necessary to change a person is to change his awareness of himself'?
meta.ogDescription: Every quote site credits Maslow. No Maslow book, paper or lecture has ever been cited — the only source offered is a 1972 children's marine-biology book.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Maslow on every quote site, and it fits his humanistic psychology — but no book, paper, lecture or letter of his has ever been produced for it. English Wikiquote lists the sentence under “Attributed,” and the single citation anyone has ever attached points not to Maslow at all but to a 1972 juvenile marine-biology book by another author.

source.heading: What the trail actually contains

docMeta.dd: William M. Stephens · McGraw-Hill, 1972 · 64 pp., juvenile marine ecology

source.excerpt: What is necessary to change a person is to change his awareness of himself.
trail: English Wikiquote files the sentence under Attributed, not among its dated, sourced Maslow quotations. Every entry in that section is referenced, if at all, to somebody else’s book rather than to Maslow’s own writing. Wikiquote: Abraham Maslow ↗

The lone citation ever attached is Life in the Open Sea (1972) by William M. Stephens, p. 21. Library cataloguing describes that title as a 64-page McGraw-Hill book on marine ecology, classified as juvenile literature and describing an open-sea food chain — not a work by Maslow, and published two years after his death in 1970. Open Library record ↗

In the revision that first put the line on Wikiquote, on 6 October 2005, it sat in the Attributed list with no citation of any kind. The Stephens reference was added to the page later. The 6 October 2005 revision ↗

The aggregators add nothing. AZQuotes reproduces the same Stephens reference; Goodreads gives the bare name with no source at all, under a standing notice that its quotes are community-submitted and unverified. Goodreads entry ↗
source.excerptNote: There is no surrounding passage to quote. The sentence circulates only as a free-standing aphorism — no located source text sits around it.
source.rightsNote: The wording’s origin is unknown, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for it. And it should not be treated as free to reuse on the assumption that it is old: Maslow’s books run from Principles of Abnormal Psychology, written with Béla Mittelmann (Harper & Brothers, 1941), through Motivation and Personality (1954) to The Farther Reaches of Human Nature (1971) — all published well inside the US copyright term, so none of it is public domain in the United States on age alone.

author.heading: Who was Abraham Maslow?
author.metaLine: 1908–1970 · American psychologist, founder of humanistic psychology
author.bio: Abraham Harold Maslow taught at Brooklyn College and then Brandeis University, where he was a professor from 1951 to 1969. He is best known for the hierarchy of needs and for Motivation and Personality (1954) and Toward a Psychology of Being (1962), the books that put self-actualization into everyday language. He died in June 1970 — and several of the lines now quoted most often as his, this one among them, are known only from books published after that.

misattribution.heading: Why the citation collapses
misattribution.intro: This line is credited to Maslow everywhere and sourced to Maslow nowhere. Three things are worth separating.

items.why: Wikiquote and AZQuotes both point at p. 21 of this book. Library records catalogue it as a 64-page McGraw-Hill title by William M. Stephens on marine ecology, shelved as juvenile literature and describing an ocean food chain from diatom to sperm whale. It is not a work by Maslow, and it appeared two years after he died. Open Library ↗

AZQuotes carries the identical Stephens reference rather than an independent one, and Goodreads offers no source whatsoever. Repetition across quote sites is not corroboration — it is one unverified claim copied many times. AZQuotes entry ↗

Even the Maslow line everyone knows is not cleanly his. Quote Investigator traces ‘if the only tool you have is a hammer’ to Maslow’s The Psychology of Science in 1966, but documents related formulations from Abraham Kaplan in 1962 and Silvan Tomkins in 1963. Quote Investigator ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The honest statement is narrow: this is a Maslow-shaped sentence with no Maslow source. Wikiquote itself files it under Attributed ↗, and nobody has yet produced a page of his that contains it.

context.heading: Why it sounds exactly like him
lead: The attribution sticks because the thought is genuinely Maslow’s territory. His psychology put a person’s own picture of themselves at the centre of the work — self-esteem sitting just below self-actualization in the hierarchy that made his name, and self-actualization framed as something a person grows into rather than something done to them. A one-line summary of that programme would sound a great deal like this sentence.

Sounding right is not the same as being sourced, though, and that is the gap the quote sites paper over. Maslow published steadily from the 1940s until his death in 1970, and his major books are all in print and searchable. If the sentence were in one of them, it would be trivial to cite — and nobody has.
detailsBody: The Wikiquote trail is instructive. The line arrived on the page in October 2005 with no source attached, in a batch of quotes an anonymous editor had lifted from the Wikipedia article. A reference was fitted to it years afterwards — and the reference it acquired was a children’s book about plankton and whales. That is what a retro-fitted citation looks like: a page number appears, but it does not lead back to the author.

None of which proves Maslow never wrote it. His output was large and includes journals, lectures and papers gathered after his death. It means only that the claim currently rests on nothing checkable, which is why this page stops at ‘attributed’ rather than reaching for ‘verified’ — or ‘disputed.’
context.pull: Sounding like Maslow is not the same as being Maslow.

sourcesVerified.claim: English Wikiquote lists "What is necessary to change a person is to change his awareness of himself" in its Attributed section, referenced to William M. Stephens, Life In the Open Sea (1972), p. 21.
The Wikiquote revision of 6 October 2005 contains the line in the Attributed section with no source citation.
Life in the open sea by William M. Stephens is a 1972 McGraw-Hill book of 64 pages, classified under marine ecology, marine biology and juvenile literature, describing an open-sea food chain.
AZQuotes gives the source for this Maslow quote as 'Life In the Open Sea'. Book by William M. Stephens (p. 21), 1972.
Goodreads attributes the line to Abraham Maslow with no book or source named, under a notice that quotes are community-added and not verified by Goodreads.

Abraham Maslow lived 1 April 1908 to 8 June 1970, was an American psychologist, professor at Brandeis 1951-1969, and published Motivation and Personality (1954), Toward a Psychology of Being (1962) and The Farther Reaches of Human Nature (1971).

Quote Investigator traces 'if the only tool you have is a hammer' to Maslow's The Psychology of Science (1966) while documenting earlier related formulations by Abraham Kaplan (1962) and Silvan Tomkins (1963).
Internet Archive holds a scan of Abraham H. Maslow, Toward a psychology of being, Van Nostrand, 1962.

Maslow's first book, Principles of Abnormal Psychology: The Dynamics of Psychic Illness, written with Bela Mittelmann, was first published by Harper & Brothers in 1941; a revised edition followed from Harper in 1951.
